web.title: Pedestrian Intention Estimation (PIE) Dataset
web.description:
PIE is a new dataset for studying pedestrian behavior in traffic. PIE contains over 6 hours of footage recorded in typical traffic scenes with on-board camera.

Rich spatial and behavioral annotations are available for pedestrians and vehicles that potentially interact with the ego-vehicle as well as for the relevant elements of infrastructure (traffic lights, signs and zebra crossings).

There are over 300K labeled video frames with 1842 pedestrian samples making this the largest publicly available dataset for studying pedestrian behavior in traffic.

## PIE Features
#### Spatial Annotations
Bounding boxes are provided for 1842 pedestrians and vehicles that interact with the driver, as well as for elements of infrastructure (traffic lights, signs, zebra crossings, road boundaries).

PIE: A Large-Scale Dataset and Models for Pedestrian Intention Estimation and Trajectory Prediction

Amir Rasouli*, Iulia Kotseruba*, Toni Kunic and John K. Tsotsos York University, Toronto, Ontario, Canada {aras,yulia,k,tk.tsotsos}@eecs.yorku.ca

Abstract

To this end, we propose a novel large-scale dataset designed for pedestrian intention estimation (PIE). We further show that combining pedestrian intention with observed motion improves trajectory prediction. The dataset and models are available at [[http://data.nvision2.eecs.yorku.ca/PIE\_dataset/](http://data.nvision2.eecs.yorku.ca/PIE\_dataset/)](http://data.nvision2.eecs.yorku.ca/PIE_dataset/).

Action prediction.

In an onboard camera setting, however, accurate depth information may not be available in many driver assistance systems.

Datasets. There are relatively few datasets that are specifically catered for pedestrian behavior prediction from a moving vehicle perspective. Publicly available pedestrian detection datasets [9, 12, 44] can potentially be used for such a purpose, however, they lack necessary characteristics such as ego-vehicle information [9], temporal correspondence [44], or enough pedestrians samples with long tracks [12]. These datasets also do not include any pedestrian observations that can be used for action prediction. A recently proposed dataset, JAAD [24], contains a large number of pedestrian samples with temporal correspondence, a subset of which are annotated with behavior information. However, for the purposes of intention estimation and trajectory prediction, this dataset has a number of drawbacks. The dataset does not have ego-vehicle information, the videos are divided into short discontinuous chunks, and the majo- rity of pedestrian samples with behavioral annotations have the intention of crossing.

Contributions. This paper offers the following four contributions: 1) A large-scale pedestrian intention estimation (PIE) dataset which includes hours of video footage of pedestrians at various types of crosswalks collected using a calibrated on-board camera. The dataset contains annotations necessary for perception and visual reasoning, including bounding boxes for traffic objects, pedestrian intentions and actions, pedestrian attributes (e.g. gender, age), road boundaries, and ego-vehicle information (e.g.

3. PIE Dataset

3.1. Data

Our dataset represents a wide diversity of pedestrian behaviors at the point of crossing and includes locations with high foot-traffic and narrow streets as well as wide boulevards with fewer pedestrians.

Annotations. Each pedestrian has a unique id and can be tracked from the moment of appearance in the scene until going out of the frame. An occlusion flag is set to partial occlusion if between 25 and 75% of the pedestrian is not visible and to full if >75% of the pedestrian is not visible.

Spatial annotations are provided for other relevant objects in the scene, including infrastructure (e.g. signs, traffic lights, zebra crossings, road boundaries) and vehicles that interact with pedestrians of interest¹.

However, this data is necessary for identifying and focusing on the most relevant pedestrians on the street, pedestrian behavior understanding and prediction, including trajectory estimation.

On the other hand, there were only 10 cases in the entire dataset where raters did not reach an agreement with respect to the pedestrian's intention, resulting in an average score of exactly 3 (Not sure'). The samples in question included pedestrians who were close to the curb or already stepped onto the road but were distracted, e.g. by their phone or by interacting with another person. However, the number of these borderline cases was very low (≈ 3%).

The PIE dataset contains 808 examples of people who intend to do but cross, 512 pedestrians with the intention to cross who eventually cross in front of the vehicle and 430 pedestrians with no crossing intention. Interestingly, there are only 2 samples where the pedestrian crossed the street but responses from human subjects did not indicate crossing intention.

The same authors who proposed the JAAD dataset also compiled another dataset called PIE (Pedestrian Intention Estimation) [[22]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b22). PIE is a larger dataset (with almost 10 times the number of frames) and contains longer pedestrian clips and better ego-vehicle information (speed, [GPS](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/physics-and-astronomy/global-positioning-system) location, heading angle). Compared to JAAD, pedestrians are more diverse in appearance, in the type of behavior they exhibit, and in their location with respect to the curb.

Compared to JAAD and PIE, PePScenes provides 3D locations of objects in the scene and a bird’s eye view semantic map.

LOKI includes different traffic scenarios collected over long collection periods under different weather conditions, road types, and [lighting conditions](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/lighting-condition), although the locations are not diverse (all scenarios were collected in central Tokyo).

## 9. Results comparison
An additional aspect hindering a [fair comparison](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/fair-comparison) of results is that many papers report their results on a single dataset. As discussed in [[166]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b166), it can become tempting for some researchers to cherry-pick a dataset where the proposed approach shines. Researchers should be encouraged to provide testing results on the two most popular datasets (JAAD and PIE) as well as on the two JAAD subsets (JAADall and JAADbeh) as done in [[25]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b25), [[32]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b32), [[58]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b58), [[59]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b59), [[60]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b60), [[63]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b63), [[67]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b67), [[68]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b68), [[72]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231224018769#b72).

## 10. Discussion and future research
### 10.1. Model generalizability
They also lack or contain few pedestrian crossing samples taken at nighttime or during adverse weather conditions (i.e. rain, snow, or fog).
